reference.source: GeneReviews / Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
clinicalPearls: Deep, longitudinal plantar and palmar furrows are the most characteristic and useful clinical clue
Intelligence ranges from normal to moderate impairment, often milder than expected for an autosomal trisomy
Facial features include a prominent forehead, deep-set eyes, a broad upturned nose, and full lips
Skeletal anomalies are common, including joint contractures, restricted movement, vertebral and rib anomalies, and absent or hypoplastic patellae
Camptodactyly and other digital anomalies are frequent
Renal, ureteric and cardiac malformations should be actively sought
Complete non-mosaic trisomy 8 is almost always lethal in utero, so survival essentially implies mosaicism
There is a recognised, though small, association with haematological malignancy that warrants awareness
reference.pathophysiology: Trisomy 8 mosaicism reflects two cell lines, one with a normal chromosome complement and one carrying an extra chromosome 8, usually arising from post-zygotic mitotic non-disjunction. Because complete trisomy 8 is incompatible with survival, the viable phenotype depends on the proportion and tissue distribution of trisomic cells, which are highly variable and explain the wide clinical spectrum. The trisomic fraction detectable in blood often falls with age, so skin fibroblast analysis may be needed, and the tissue-limited nature accounts for the frequently milder-than-expected outcome.
additionalDifferentials: Overgrowth and connective-tissue syndromes featuring deep palmar or plantar creases
Distal arthrogryposis syndromes, for the contractures
Isolated congenital heart or renal malformation syndromes
Other dysmorphology syndromes such as Kabuki syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Blood karyotype, but with a low threshold for skin fibroblast or buccal karyotype and FISH because blood mosaicism may be low or lost
Chromosomal microarray, recognising low-level mosaicism can be missed
Skeletal and spinal imaging for vertebral and patellar anomalies
Awareness of and surveillance for haematological abnormalities
redFlags: Features of a haematological malignancy such as unexplained cytopenias or bruising
Progressive renal impairment from a structural anomaly
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally more favourable than for most autosomal trisomies, with many individuals having normal or only mildly impaired intellect; prognosis depends chiefly on the severity of associated malformations and on any haematological complication.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis on a normal blood karyotype without testing fibroblasts
Missing the fall in blood mosaicism that occurs with age
Overlooking the recognised association with haematological disease
Underrecognising the diagnostic value of deep plantar furrows
references: Smith's Recognizable Patterns of Human Malformation
management: Screen for and manage renal, ureteric and cardiac malformations with imaging-guided surgical or medical correction as needed
Provide orthopaedic and physiotherapy management of joint contractures, vertebral and patellar anomalies and restricted movement
Offer developmental support and early intervention tailored to the degree of intellectual impairment
Maintain haematological surveillance given the recognised association of trisomy 8 with myelodysplasia and myeloid leukaemia
Coordinate multidisciplinary follow-up across cardiology, nephrology, orthopaedics and developmental paediatrics
Offer genetic counselling, noting the usually sporadic post-zygotic origin and low recurrence risk
